item.title: ‘Kraft Dinner’ budget: Mayor’s comments prompt second protest at City Hall
item.description: Protesters gathered in front of City Hall Thursday afternoon to protest comments made by Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.
item.dc:creator: Daniel J. Rowe, Matt Gilmour
item.content:encoded: After starting a swirl of memes, mockery and malcontent over Kraft Dinner comments, protesters gathered in front of City Hall Thursday afternoon to protest Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada. A protest began at 1 p.m. following the nearly 10 per cent tax increase announced earlier this week, followed by Martinez Ferrada’s since walked-back statements. “It’s just like when you’re putting together your personal budget: If you know you’re going to have less money next year, well, you have to make some choices,” she said in a Quartre95 interview. “Let’s be honest, maybe sometimes we’ll eat a little more Kraft Dinner because we can’t afford filet mignon.” The mayor recorded a social media post the following day saying “it was pretty tactless.” “What I meant was that when a city makes choices, it’s the same as when you make personal choices,” she said. “In this instance, the city has to choose between paying for new parks or filling potholes, and I’m going to choose filling potholes.” Protesters came armed with Kraft Dinner, pans, stoves and ingredients, with the apparent intention to make the Canadian household staple a political flashpoint. Raúl Garate organized the protest, saying the tax hike will affect home owners, but also tenants. “I’m not against the fact that we need to take care of our of our city because it is in dire need of love,” he said, adding that he was concerned about the burden on working Montrealers. “You have people, like working-class people, that struggle so much to make their ends meet that will have to also consider this new tax hike.” Montreal’s budget increased the average municipal tax rate to 9.8 per cent in Montreal. It was the largest increase in 50 years. Martinez Ferrada said the increase was necessary to deal with the city’s aging infrastructure, including water mains, housing and homelessness. Protesters fear the nearly 10 per cent tax hikes will be passed on to renters and hurt the most vulnerable in society. “Life in Montreal has gotten increasingly expensive, and the comments made by our mayor were beyond unacceptable,” one protester said. Signs depicting the mayor as Marie Antoinette illustrate the sense here that Martinez Ferrada is out of touch. “It was completely, not just tone deaf, but it shows the disconnect that she has from Montrealers,” said another protester. So many memes Hundreds of viral memes about the Kraft Dinner comments have flooded social media. One expert said this type of content has become a powerful form of political discourse. “Memes add to the conversation and they add to the feeling of momentum around a politician or an issue. And sometimes that is good momentum, and sometimes that is not so good momentum,” said Colleen McCool, a Concordia University political communications student. There’s even a website that breaks down the city budget line by line costed out in terms of boxes of Kraft Dinner showing this year’s total spending equal to 3.5 billion boxes. “I just kind of wanted to use this moment as a hook to show this data in an interesting way. To have citizens kind of exploring this data, reasoning about it, asking like, is this how I picture the budget should be spent?” said Niko Draca, creator of kdgate.ca. Outside City Hall, many feel the administrations’ priorities are wrong. “To give $45 million more to the police and raise our taxes by 10 per cent. That’s a choice. We didn’t choose that,” said a protester. Thursday’s protest was the second one to take place this week, as hundreds of demonstrators gathered on Tuesday. Peter Sergakis, owner of hundreds of residential units, bars and restaurants, organized that protest.

item.title: Global stocks rise and tech shares rebound as U.S. closes for Thanksgiving
item.description: U.S. stock futures also climbed, with the S&P 500 futures up 0.5 per cent. U.S. markets will reopen Friday for a holiday-shortened session.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: HONG KONG — Shares advanced in Europe and Asia on Thursday while U.S. markets were closed for the Thanksgiving holiday. Buying of stocks tied to artificial intelligence helped push benchmarks in Asia higher, though some profit-taking by investors toward the end of the day pared those gains. Investors have been growing cautious about the AI trade. They also are watching for impacts from the latest tariff hikes Washington plans to impose on China, Japan, the European Union and other trading partners. In early European trading, Germany’s DAX jumped 1.9 per cent to 25,180.12, while France’s CAC 40 climbed 1.8 per cent to 8,126.47. Britain’s FTSE 100 added 1.6 per cent to 10,591.83. U.S. stock futures also climbed, with the S&P 500 futures up 0.5 per cent. U.S. markets will reopen Friday for a holiday-shortened session. In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 rebounded and closed 0.9 per cent higher at 57,499.16. OpenAI investor SoftBank Group jumped 7.3 per cent, while memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings surged 12.6 per cent. Shares of chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron were up 0.6 per cent. South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index added 0.3 per cent to 4,711.21 after a 6.2 per cent drop a day earlier. Samsung Electronics gained 0.4 per cent, while memory chipmaker SK Hynix rose 2.2 per cent. Taiwan’s Taiex was 2.5 per cent higher. But shares of its leading chipmaker TSMC, or Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., edged 0.2 per cent lower. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index was 1.2 per cent higher at 22,226.88. The Shanghai Composite index was up less than 0.1 per cent at 3,476.88. Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 gained 0.8 per cent to 8,763.80. India’s Sensex rose 0.5 per cent. Wall Street closed mixed ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. The benchmark S&P 500 index lost 0.3 per cent Wednesday after falling as much as 3.2 per cent earlier in the day. The technology-heavy Nasdaq composite closed 0.6 per cent lower, after recovering from a drop of as much as 4.6 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average picked up 0.3 per cent. Nvidia fell 3.9 per cent as AI shares lost steam for a second day after Jensen Huang’s comeback as CEO. On Wednesday, S&P Global Ratings warned it could downgrade Nvidia’s credit rating over concerns surrounding its management and governance. Broadcom, which had fallen sharply earlier in the day, was 0.1 per cent lower at the close. Anthropic, which began public trading last week, recovered from an early drop and ended 1.1 per cent higher, though still below its IPO, or initial public offering, price of US$83 per share. In commodities trading, oil prices climbed early Thursday as tensions in the Middle East persisted even as global oil supply continued to recover. Brent crude, the international standard, was 0.5 per cent higher at $91.09 per barrel. It was trading at approximately $72 a barrel before the war began in late February. Benchmark U.S. crude gained one per cent to $84.51 per barrel. Recent reports of vessels being targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway for global oil transport, have contributed to concerns over oil flows and “brought supply risks back into focus,” ING commodities strategists Ewa Manthey and Warren Patterson said in a commentary Thursday. The U.S. dollar rose to 159.30 Japanese yen from 159.16 yen. The euro was trading at $1.0968, down from $1.0974. Chan Ho-him, The Associated Press

item.title: Auto sector in Canada is moving away from U.S. imports: DesRosiers
item.description: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: A new report suggests the Canadian auto sector is starting to pivot away from U.S. imports toward other global markets amid the ongoing trade war. The data analysis from DesRosiers Automotive Consultants showed that light vehicle imports from the United States have accounted for 40 per cent of Canada’s total thus far in 2026 when measured by dollars. That result is down from 49.1 per cent of Canada’s light vehicle imports in 2024. Meanwhile, most other markets saw their shares rise from two years ago. The proportion of Canada’s light vehicle imports from Mexico increased from 16.7 per cent in 2024 to 20.5 per cent so far this year, while Japan saw an increase to 12.9 per cent from 10.7 per cent in 2024. Imports from South Korea have risen from 10.4 to 12.5 per cent, and the combined European markets saw a bump from 9.8 to 11.1 per cent. Aside from Canada’s southern neighbour, China was the only market behind its 2024 share at 2.6 per cent thus far in 2026, down from 2.9 per cent. The overall shift is notable given that not all manufacturers are affected by Canada’s counter-tariffs, which exclude some of the highest volume players, the report said. DesRosiers managing partner Andrew King said certain manufacturers affected by the tariff situation “have moved rapidly to seek other sourcing where possible and to continue to provide Canadians with vehicles at the best possible price.” “What the U.S. lost in share was captured readily by the other major light vehicle exporters, with the trade war helping to diversify Canada’s sourcing in this space,” he said in a statement. Vehicles made in Canada are tariffed by the United States at 25 per cent, minus their American content, while auto and truck parts that comply with the Canada-United States-Mexico agreement on trade are exempt.  In August, President Donald Trump threatened to hike tariffs on all vehicles, auto parts and steel from Canada to 50 per cent on Jan. 1. Canada maintains import duties of 25 per cent on U.S. autos that are not compliant with CUSMA. Ottawa allows automakers to import a quota of vehicles made in the United States tariff-free, based in part on their level of automotive assembly in Canada. Automotive analyst Daniel Ross said the figures show manufacturers are “fighting ... to keep prices from climbing.” “I think it’s directly related to trade policy and the trade war at hand,” said Ross, senior manager of auto industry insights at Canadian Black Book. “A lot of manufacturers are finding their way to decrease dependency for the Canadian market based off of what’s happening in the U.S. So the narrative is, ultimately, where else can we get these? Where is it easier? Where can we work with?” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in recent weeks that trade talks with the U.S. are making progress, but Ottawa won’t accept a deal that doesn’t allow for a viable auto sector. That came three months after Canada pulled out of trade talks with the U.S. due to last-minute demands from Washington that included a hit to Canada’s auto sector. Whether automakers continue to shift imports to non-U.S. markets will depend on how trade negotiations progress, said Ross. “If it were not to move (in a positive) direction, then I think we could continue to see that climb of market share for Mexico, for Japan specifically,” he said. “Whether or not that’s the best way forward, it’s a better way forward than having our skin in the game with a U.S. marketplace that’s highly volatile for the last few years.” --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 25, 2026.
